metaDescription: Seven gasoline cans and fuel caddies for generators compared by capacity, spout design, safety features and handling, from 2 gallon cans to 15 gallon caddies.
expertTake: The Scepter 5 gallon SmartControl can is the best all-round choice because it holds a full generator refill and pours without glugging. The Eagle 5 gallon Type I safety can is the pick for owners who want metal and a flame arrester. If your generator runs more than a day between refills, skip small cans and buy a wheeled caddy.
introParagraphs: Fuel storage is the part of generator ownership people forget until the engine coughs in the middle of an outage. A good container keeps gasoline fresh, pours without spilling and stores safely until you need it.

Cans differ in capacity, spout design, material and whether they carry fire-safety hardware. Larger caddies move more fuel with wheels and a pump, but they are for transfer and short storage, and they demand a stricter location and handling routine.

products.name: Scepter 5-gal SmartControl gas can, EPA/CARB compliant
products.description:
The spout is the design point: a squeeze-control SmartControl nozzle with an integrated air vent lets fuel flow in a steady stream and stops when you release it. That removes the glug and splash of older cans, and the included funnel and spout extender help when the generator's fill neck is recessed.

Five gallons is the practical size for a portable generator. It holds about one full refill of a mid-size tank and weighs roughly 30 pounds when full, which is about the limit most people can lift and pour comfortably. Next to the 2 gallon Scepter, it halves the number of trips; next to a 15 gallon caddy, it stays lifting-friendly.

The resin is high-density polyethylene, so it will not rust or dent. Keep it in the shade, because heat softens plastic and raises internal pressure. Check the spout seal at the start of each season and replace the can if the neck is cracked or the gasket is hardened. Before a storm, fill the cans you plan to use, add stabiliser to any fuel older than a few months and label each can with the fill date. Pouring is easier if you rest the spout on the tank neck and let the vent work, rather than squeezing hard.
products.bestFor: Most portable generators with a 3 to 5 gallon tank.
pros: HDPE will not rust or dent
Spout extender helps recessed tank necks
cons: Squeeze spout needs a firm grip when full

products.name: Eagle 5-gal Type I safety gas can with flame arrester
products.description:
A Type I safety can has a single opening for filling and pouring, a self-closing gasketed cap and a non-sparking flame arrester in the neck. The arrester is a mesh that keeps a flashback from reaching the fuel inside, which is the reason these cans are common on job sites.

The seam is a double interlock with no weld on the bottom, and the handle is fixed. It includes an F-15 funnel for filling. That makes it a better long-term container than plastic where fire safety rules are strict.

The tradeoff is pouring. A single-opening can needs a funnel and a steady hand, and it can glug if the stream is not controlled. It also dents and, over many years, rusts at the seams if it lives in a damp shed. Compared with the plastic Scepter, it is also more resistant to fuel permeation, which matters if the can sits for a year. Wipe it dry after rain and keep the arrester clear of debris, since a clogged mesh slows the pour.
products.bestFor: Owners who want metal construction and a flame arrester.
cons: Single opening can glug without a funnel
Metal can dent and rust over time

products.name: Scepter 2-gal SmartControl gas can, EPA/CARB compliant
products.description:
The two gallon can uses the same squeeze-control spout as the five gallon model, with a five-layer high-density polyethylene wall that resists corrosion, denting and breakage. It is light enough to carry in one hand when full, about 12 to 13 pounds.

For a small inverter generator with a one to two gallon tank, this is the more sensible size, because you are rarely pouring more than a gallon at a time. It also suits owners who cannot lift a five gallon can safely.

The downside is trips and storage. During a multi-day outage a two gallon can runs out quickly, so keep two or three on hand or step up to the five gallon size. Its handle sits near the spout, which suits a smooth one-handed pour, and the five-layer wall tolerates being tossed in a truck bed better than thin plastic. Keep one dedicated to the generator and mark it, so the contents are never in doubt.
products.bestFor: Small inverter generators and anyone who struggles with heavy cans.
pros: Same controllable spout as the 5 gallon size
Easy to store in a small shed
cons: Runs out quickly in a long outage
More trips to the pump than larger cans

products.name: No Spill 1405 2.5-gal gasoline can
products.description:
A thumb button controls the pour, which keeps flow steady and lets you stop instantly. The 7/8 inch funnel spout is slim enough to fit small equipment inlets, and an attached dust cover keeps the spout clean.

At 2.5 gallons it sits between the two gallon and five gallon Scepter cans. That size is comfortable to lift and gives a little more runtime than a two gallon can.

The design is a different philosophy from squeeze spouts: you press a button rather than squeeze the body. Owners with weak hands may find the button easier, while others prefer a squeeze. Keep the dust cover closed so grit does not scratch the seal. Because the can is shorter than a five gallon model, it stores easily on a low shelf and pours cleanly into a generator with a low fuel door. Over time the button spring and seal are the wear points, so test the stop action each season before you rely on it.
products.bestFor: Owners who prefer a button-controlled pour in a mid-small size.
pros: Attached dust cover protects the spout
2.5 gallon size is easy to lift
cons: Smaller than a full 5 gallon refill
Button mechanism has more parts than a simple cap

products.name: MAXSA 15-gal fuel caddy with manual pump and 10 ft hose
products.description:
A 15 gallon caddy moves a lot of fuel on wheels and uses a manual pump with a 10 foot hose to move it into a generator tank. The reinforced LLDPE tank is described as resistant to UV, corrosion and impact, and there is an adjustable air vent and a brass fitting for smooth flow.

At 15 gallons the container holds about three generator refills, which suits a multi-day outage or a job site. Full, it weighs around 90 pounds, so it must be wheeled, not lifted.

The tradeoff is storage and risk. A large volume of gasoline in a plastic tank should sit in a ventilated outbuilding, not a living area, and you should follow local limits on stored fuel. Fill it only as much as you can use in a reasonable time. Prime the pump hose with a few strokes before you start, and keep the hose end below the tank opening to avoid backflow. After use, drain the hose and cap it so fuel does not sit in the line.
products.bestFor: Long outages or job sites where one trip should cover several refills.
pros: Wheels make 90 lb full weight manageable
cons: Large fuel volume demands careful storage

products.name: 15-gal fuel caddy with siphon pump, 10 ft hose, wheeled
products.description:
The listing describes two modes: a manual siphon pump and a gravity drive for refuelling. Six-inch wheels and a top handle make it easy to move from the garage to the generator.

At 15 gallons it matches the MAXSA caddy on size, so the choice between them is about pump design and listing detail. A siphon system fills slower than a gravity feed when the caddy sits on a raised platform.

Because gravity feed needs the caddy to sit higher than the tank, plan a safe platform. Keep it clear of the generator's hot exhaust and never refuel a running or hot engine. A raised platform also helps when the generator's fill neck is below the caddy's outlet, since gravity then does the work and you only have to watch the level. Keep a small spill kit nearby, such as absorbent pads, because even careful transfers drip.
products.bestFor: Owners who want gravity and siphon modes in one wheeled caddy.
pros: Top handle helps lifting onto a truck
cons: Gravity mode needs a raised platform

products.name: Scepter Duramax Flo 'N Go 14-gal gas caddy
products.description:
The Flo 'N Go is a fuel tank on wheels with 6-inch wheels and a heavy-duty top handle. It offers two fueling modes: gravity-flow when elevated above the tank being filled, and a pump mode for lower targets.

At 14 gallons it is a notch below the 15 gallon caddies, which matters little in practice. It comes from a brand that already makes the five gallon can at the top of this list, so spare parts and documentation are easy to find.

Treat it as a transfer vehicle, not long-term storage. Fill it only for the job, keep it in a ventilated place and drain unused fuel into approved cans before winter. Check the wheels and axle each season, since a caddy that wobbles under 90 pounds is a tip-over risk. Compared with the 15 gallon models, the capacity difference is small, so choose by pump or gravity preference and by whether you value an established accessory range.
products.bestFor: Owners who want a caddy from a known can maker.
cons: Fuel left in plastic for months can degrade

buyingCriteria.explanation: A full 5 gallon can weighs about 30 pounds, a 2 gallon can about 13 pounds, and a 15 gallon caddy about 90. Match the size to what you can lift and pour. A heavy can you struggle with is a spill waiting to happen.
Squeeze spouts like the Scepter SmartControl, and thumb-button spouts like the No Spill 1405, limit splashing. A Type I safety can needs a funnel. Pick the pour style you can control with one hand.
HDPE cans such as the Scepter will not rust but soften in heat. A metal Type I can like the Eagle adds a flame arrester. Choose by where it will live and what local rules require.
EPA and CARB compliance, stated on the Scepter cans, means a spill-proof, sealed design. It pours slower than older cans, and compliance is mandatory in many states. Look for the label.
Red cans are for gasoline and yellow for diesel by convention. The Scepter diesel can in yellow is not for a gasoline generator. Mixing fuels can wreck an engine, so keep cans marked.

The MAXSA and 15 gallon caddies offer manual pumps with 10 foot hoses, and the Scepter Flo 'N Go offers gravity flow. A pump works from the ground, while gravity needs a platform. Choose the method you can set up safely.

howWeEvaluated.title: Pour control
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared squeeze, thumb-button and funnel designs, noting spill risk for each. The Scepter SmartControl and No Spill 1405 offer controllable pours. The Eagle needs a funnel.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity fit
howWeEvaluated.description: We matched can sizes to generator tanks: 2 and 2.5 gallon for small inverters, 5 gallon for mid-size portables, and 14 to 15 gallon caddies for long outages. Bigger is not better if you cannot move it.

howWeEvaluated.title: Safety hardware
howWeEvaluated.description: We credited flame arresters, self-closing caps and EPA and CARB compliance. These are listing facts, not claims about a particular accident. We drew this from listed specifications and common buyer reports.

howWeEvaluated.title: Material durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared HDPE and metal, and noted UV resistance on the MAXSA caddy. Plastic resists rust but not heat. Metal resists heat but not rust.

howWeEvaluated.title: Transfer method
howWeEvaluated.description: We separated cans that pour from caddies that pump or gravity feed. The right method depends on how high your generator tank sits.

rows: Want metal and a flame arrester

cards.label: Plastic can
cards.text: The Scepter cans resist rust and dents and are light, and their spouts pour cleanly. They soften in strong heat and can permeate over years.

cards.label: Metal can
cards.text: The Eagle Type I can adds a flame arrester and resists heat. It dents, can rust in damp sheds and needs a funnel to pour.

howToChoose.note: Choose plastic for easy pouring and metal if local rules or your preference call for a safety can.

rows: Want a button instead of squeeze

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Enough volume for several refills, a wheeled or pumped transfer, a stabiliser plan and a safe storage place. Fuel stored for months needs stabiliser and rotation.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The MAXSA 15 gallon caddy and the 15 gallon siphon caddy hold about three refills, and the Scepter Flo 'N Go adds a gravity mode.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You run a generator for days at a time or need metal safety hardware, pointing to a 15 gallon caddy or the Eagle can.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You run a small inverter for a few hours, where the Scepter 2 gallon can is enough.

maintenance.why: A hardened gasket leaks vapour and fuel. Replace the can if the seal will not close.
Ethanol blends absorb water and degrade over months. Stabiliser extends useful life.
Burn old fuel in a car and refill with fresh. A can of stale gas can gum a carburettor.
UV and impact weaken plastic, and dents weaken metal seams. Retire damaged cans.
Debris blocks the vent and slows flow. A clear vent also prevents glugging.

faq.q: What size fuel can should I buy for a generator?
faq.a: A 5 gallon can suits most mid-size portables. A 2 gallon can suits small inverter generators and anyone who cannot lift heavy loads. Caddies suit multi-day outages.

faq.q: How long can I store gasoline for a generator?
faq.a: Untreated gasoline can degrade in a few months, and ethanol blends absorb water. With stabiliser it can last about a year in a sealed can. Rotate it into a vehicle and refill with fresh fuel.

faq.q: Is a metal or plastic can safer?
faq.a: Both can be safe if they are the right type and in good condition. Metal Type I cans add a flame arrester, and plastic cans resist rust. Follow local storage rules and keep cans out of living spaces.

faq.q: Why do new gas cans pour slowly?
faq.a: EPA and CARB compliant cans use sealed, self-closing spouts that vent through the nozzle. They pour slower than old vented cans. Squeeze or button controls help, and a firm seat on the tank neck reduces spills.

faq.q: Can I use a diesel can for gasoline?
faq.a: No. Cans are colour coded by convention, with yellow for diesel. Use a red can for gasoline and never mix fuels.

faq.q: Is it safe to refuel a running generator?
faq.a: No. Shut the engine off and let it cool before refueling, because spilled gasoline on a hot engine can ignite. Fill outdoors, away from ignition sources.
